meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No one can make you feel inferior without your consent'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Eleanor Roosevelt for 80+ years, yet found in nothing she wrote — it first appears unsourced in a 1940 Reader's Digest. An honest 'attributed.'

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1884–1962 · U.S. First Lady, diplomat & human-rights advocate
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Eleanor Roosevelt, the line is consistent with — and almost certainly grew out of — her documented 1935 remark that “a snub is the effort of a person who feels superior to make someone else feel inferior.” But the polished sentence appears in none of her books, columns or speeches; its earliest known print is an unsourced 1940 Reader’s Digest filler line ↗, so no primary source pins it to her.

source.heading: What Roosevelt actually said
source.excerpt: No one can make you feel inferior without your consent.
trail: The Quote Investigator ↗ found the earliest attribution to Roosevelt in Reader’s Digest, September 1940 — a stand-alone line with no source given.
Its documented seed is her 1935 press-conference remark ↗ about a snub, reported by the Associated Press.
A strikingly similar sentiment predates her: clergyman William Ellery Channing wrote in 1838 ↗ that no hardship “can depress you … but by your own consent.”
Despite thorough searches, the exact wording appears in none of her books or archived writings ↗ — which is why the credit stays ‘attributed,’ not verified.
source.cutTag: ↑ the polished line is a later distillation, not a documented quotation
source.excerptNote: The nearest thing to a documented source is Eleanor Roosevelt’s own 1935 comment on a diplomatic snub, reported by the Associated Press: “A snub is the effort of a person who feels superior to make someone else feel inferior. To do so, he has to find someone who can be made to feel inferior.” The compact modern aphorism seems to have been distilled from this — by an unknown hand — sometime before 1940.
source.rightsNote: As a short aphorism the sentence carries no meaningful copyright, and its 1935 documented root was a public press-conference remark. Note that no verified author exists for the polished wording — it is best cited as “attributed to Eleanor Roosevelt,” not as a sourced quotation.

author.name: Eleanor Roosevelt
author.heading: About Eleanor Roosevelt
author.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt (1884–1962) was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, redefining the role across Franklin D. Roosevelt’s four terms (1933–1945). After his death she chaired the UN commission that drove the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights, earning the nickname “First Lady of the World.” She wrote the daily “My Day” column from the mid-1930s until her death — the very corpus in which the famous aphorism, tellingly, does not appear.

context.heading: The gap between what she said and what she’s quoted as saying
lead: Few lines are quoted more confidently — or documented more thinly. The sentence is a fixture of graduation speeches and self-help posters, almost always stamped with Eleanor Roosevelt’s name, yet researchers have never located it in anything she is known to have written or said.

What she did say, at a 1935 White House press conference, was a sharper, more clinical observation about snobbery: that a snub only works if its target agrees to feel small. Somewhere in the next five years an anonymous editor smoothed that thought into the memorable maxim we know — and handed the credit back to her.
detailsBody: The same idea, in gentler dress, appears a century earlier ↗ in the writing of Unitarian clergyman William Ellery Channing (1838), a sign the sentiment was in the air long before it acquired Roosevelt’s name.
